claims.text: Configurational disorder in high-entropy superconducting alloys produces local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions primarily govern superconducting behavior by modulating electron–phonon coupling.
Reducing local lattice distortions strengthens electron–phonon coupling.
Reduced local lattice distortions yield a higher superconducting transition temperature.
Reduced local lattice distortions yield a sharper superconducting transition.
Enhanced disorder increases electron scattering that acts as a Cooper-pair breaker.
Thermal annealing can reduce local lattice distortions without changing the alloy's overall chemical composition.
XRD peak broadening can quantify the degree of lattice distortion or strain.
TEM or EXAFS bond-length variations can quantify local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortions alter the phonon spectrum.
Local lattice distortions shift the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes to the phonon spectrum and Fermi-level density of states caused by lattice distortion reduce the electron–phonon coupling constant.
Annealing minimizes pair-breaking scattering by reducing lattice distortions.
Annealed samples with demonstrably reduced lattice distortion will have higher critical current density than as-cast samples.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase, chemically homogeneous high-entropy superconductors in which disorder-induced lattice distortion is the primary changed variable.
Secondary phases, magnetic impurities, or strong electron-correlation effects may dominate superconducting behavior and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Magnetic impurities and microstructural inhomogeneities could provide additional scattering mechanisms that influence Tc.
Failure to observe a statistically significant improvement in Tc, transition sharpness, or critical current density correlated with reduced distortion would reject the hypothesis.
